title: Gods Who Must Be Carried and the God Who Carries
summary: The great gods of Babylon, Bel and Nebo, are pictured as heavy statues loaded onto weary animals and hauled away into captivity. In contrast, the LORD reminds Israel that he has carried them from birth and will carry them into old age. He mocks the gods that must be bought, made, and carried and yet cannot answer, and declares that he announces the end from the beginning and will accomplish his purpose through a man from the east, bringing his salvation near to Zion.
story: Chapters 40 to 45 argued that the LORD alone is God and named Cyrus as his instrument. Chapter 46 brings the argument to the gods of Babylon themselves, naming two of the most important. In chapter 47 Babylon the city will fall; here its gods fall first. The chapter is short, but it contains one of the most memorable contrasts in Scripture: idols are a burden their worshipers must carry, while the living God carries his people. The exiles, tempted to be impressed by Babylon's splendid religion, are called to remember who has been carrying them all along.
historical:
Bel was a title meaning lord, used in this period for Marduk, the patron god of Babylon and head of its pantheon. Nebo is Nabu, Marduk's son, god of writing and wisdom, whose chief temple stood at Borsippa near Babylon. The kings of Babylon bore names honoring these gods: Nebuchadnezzar and Nabonidus contain the name of Nabu, and Belshazzar contains Bel. Each spring at the New Year festival, the statue of Nabu was brought from Borsippa to Babylon, and the images of the gods were carried in great processions. The last Babylonian king, Nabonidus, spent years away from the city in Arabia, and Babylonian records note that the festival was not held during his absence, which alienated many in Babylon.

As Cyrus approached in 539 BC, Babylonian records state that Nabonidus brought the statues of gods from other cities into Babylon, presumably to protect them. After his victory, Cyrus sent them back. Cyrus himself honored Marduk rather than carrying him off, so the image of Bel and Nebo loaded onto animals and taken into captivity is best read as a poetic picture of the gods' helplessness, not a description of a single event (see the hard question below).
cultural:
In the ancient Near East, the images of the gods were moved by carts and pack animals or on the shoulders of priests, both in festival processions and in times of war. A conquering army often carried off the statues of a defeated city's gods as trophies, and a city that lost its gods had suffered the deepest humiliation. Assyrian reliefs show soldiers carrying away captured divine statues. The exiles would have seen the Babylonian processions and known what it meant to see a god hauled out of a city.

The process of making a god, described in verses 6 and 7, was costly. Worshipers weighed out gold and silver (coins were not yet in wide use, so metal was measured by weight on scales), hired a goldsmith, and then carried the finished statue to its shrine, where it stayed exactly where it was put. The contrast with the living God depends on those details: the idols cost money, need carrying, and stand still.
literary: The chapter is built on a play of verbs. The same words for carrying and bearing (nasa and saval) are used for the idols, which must be carried, and for God, who carries his people. The idols are a load on weary animals (verse 1); God has borne Israel from the womb (verse 3). The pairing is sharpest in verse 4, where God says in five short clauses that he will be the same, bear, carry, sustain, and deliver. The rest of the chapter uses the familiar forms of these chapters: a comparison question (“To whom will you liken Me”), a satire of idol-making, and a summons to remember, closing with an address to the “stubborn people” that God will save anyway.

outline.t: Bel and Nebo carried away as a burden
The LORD who carries his people from birth to old age
The god that must be bought, made, and carried
Remember: God declares the end from the beginning
Salvation brought near to stubborn Zion

doctrines.note: God carries his people through every stage of life: “Even to your old age, I will be the same, and I will bear you up when you turn gray.” Providence here is personal care, not a distant system.
“I declare the end from the beginning.” God's purpose stands, and he carries it out through events and people, including the man from the east. What he plans, he does.
An idol is something we make and then must carry. The chapter's diagnosis is that false gods always become burdens, demanding costly service and giving nothing back.
God brings his righteousness and salvation near to a people who are “far removed from righteousness.” The rescue does not wait for Israel to become worthy.

words.note: Saval, to bear a heavy load. It appears twice in verse 4 for God carrying his people and once in verse 7 for worshipers shouldering their idol. The same verb appears in Isaiah 53:4 and 53:11, where the Servant bears the sorrows and iniquities of others. What God does for his people here, the Servant will do in the deepest way.

Bel, meaning lord, the title of Marduk, chief god of Babylon. His temple, the Esagila, dominated the city, and the creation epic recited in his honor celebrated his supremacy. Isaiah pictures this supreme god crouching under his own weight.

Acharit, end or latter part. “I declare the end from the beginning.” The word refers to the outcome of events, what things come to. God sees and announces the outcome before it begins, which is the proof the idols could never give.
Etsah, counsel or purpose. “My purpose will stand.” The word describes a plan formed by deliberation. The man from the east is “a man for My purpose,” the instrument of God's settled counsel.

christ: The chapter's central contrast, gods who must be carried and a God who carries, finds its fullest expression in the gospel. The verb used here for God bearing his people is the same one used in Isaiah 53 for the Servant who “carried our sorrows” and bears the iniquities of many, and the New Testament identifies that Servant with Jesus (for example Matthew 8:17 and 1 Peter 2:24). Jesus's invitation to the weary and burdened to come to him for rest (Matthew 11:28-30) stands in the same line: where false gods add to our burdens, the true God lifts them. The claim that God declares the end from the beginning also shapes the New Testament's conviction that the death and resurrection of Jesus happened according to God's plan and foreknowledge (Acts 2:23). These links are thematic, drawn from the wider story rather than predictions in this chapter.

hard.q: Babylon's gods were not actually carried off when Cyrus took the city. Did this prophecy fail?
hard.a:
It is true that Cyrus did not take Marduk into captivity. His own inscription presents him as Marduk's chosen king, and he restored the gods that Nabonidus had brought into the city to their home temples. Readers have responded in several ways. Many interpreters read the chapter as poetry, not prediction of a specific event: the picture of gods loaded on animals is a vivid way of saying that the gods of Babylon cannot save their city or themselves. On this reading, the point was fulfilled when Babylon fell without its gods lifting a finger. Others note that the gods of cities were routinely carried about, whether for festivals, for protection, or as spoils, and that Nabonidus's own gathering of gods into Babylon was already a scene of gods hauled about in fear. Some also point out that Babylon's gods were later humiliated when the Persian king Xerxes, according to Greek sources, removed a great statue from Babylon after a revolt, though the details are debated.

The chapter's lasting point does not depend on one event. Gods made by human hands have to be carried, and when disaster comes they go wherever their carriers go.

questions: The idols were a burden to those who carried them. What in your life feels like a god you have to keep carrying?
God promises to carry his people even into old age and gray hair. How does that promise speak to fears about growing old?
God brings salvation near to a “stubborn people.” What does it mean to you that God's rescue does not wait for us to deserve it?
